english: Your parcel's here / A delivery came
usage: 존댓말 — courier or family member announcing a delivery
반말 — to a friend, roommate, or younger family member
격식 — an app/SMS notification or a building intercom announcement
There's a delivery — can you come get it?
Courier at the door checking if you can receive it now
examples:
택배 왔어요.
네, 감사합니다.
Your parcel's here. — Yes, thank you.
The bare announcement and the natural one-word reply
어, 택배 왔나 봐. 누가 좀 받아 줘.
Oh, looks like a delivery came. Someone grab it.
왔나 봐 = 'looks like it came', guessing from the doorbell
택배 왔는데 지금 집에 아무도 없어서요. 경비실에 맡겨 주시겠어요?
A parcel came but nobody's home right now. Could you leave it at the security office?
Real situation: redirecting a delivery you can't receive
nuance: This is the everyday phrase for 'a package arrived', said by a courier (택배 기사님) at your door, by a family member who heard the bell, or by an app push. 택배 means a courier/parcel-delivery service, so 택배 왔어요 literally is 'the delivery came'. To a stranger-courier you keep 존댓말 (왔어요); inside the family it drops to 반말 (왔어), and an automated notice uses the stiff 도착했습니다. The nearest alternative is 배송 왔어요, but 배송 is the abstract 'shipping' process word (used by stores: 배송 시작/배송 완료) while 택배 is the physical parcel and the human who brings it — say 택배 for the box at your door. English speakers often try to translate 'the delivery guy is here' word-for-word as 배달원이 있어요, which sounds robotic; Koreans just say 택배 왔어요 or call the person 택배 기사님. Also note 배달 (with ㄹ) means hot food delivery (pizza, chicken), not parcels — don't mix 택배 and 배달.

mistakes: Saying 배달 왔어요 for a parcel — 배달 is food delivery (치킨, 피자); a courier box is 택배, so the bell-ring announcement is 택배 왔어요.
Calling the courier 택배맨 or 배달원 to their face — the polite term is 택배 기사님 (driver-sir); 기사님 shows respect.
Using 배송 for the box itself (배송 왔어요 sounds off) — 배송 is the shipping process; the arrived parcel is 택배.

english: Please leave it at the door
usage: Please leave it at the door.
존댓말 — to a courier; standard contactless-delivery request
Just leave it by the door.
반말 — to a friend or family member dropping something off
You can just leave it at the door, thank you.
격식/정중 — fuller, very polite written or spoken request
You can just leave it at the door and go.
Natural extension telling the courier they needn't wait
examples:
문 앞에 놔 주세요.
네, 알겠습니다.
Please leave it at the door. — Sure, got it.
The core request and the courier's standard reply
지금 손이 안 비어서요. 그냥 문 앞에 놔 주세요.
My hands are full right now. Just leave it at the door, please.
그냥 = 'just', softens it to 'no need to hand it over'
벨 누르지 마시고 문 앞에 놔 주세요. 아기가 자고 있어서요.
Please don't ring the bell, just leave it at the door — the baby's sleeping.
Real note added in a delivery-app request box (배송 요청사항)
nuance: This is the contactless-delivery line you say to a courier or type into the app's 요청사항 (request) box. 놔 주세요 is the contracted spoken form of 놓아 주세요 ('please place it'); both are correct — 놔 주세요 in speech, 놓아 주세요 in careful writing. To a stranger-courier use 주세요 (존댓말); among family it becomes 놔 줘. The near-synonym is 두고 가세요 ('leave it and go'), which adds the nuance that they don't need to wait for you; 놔 주세요 just specifies the spot. English speakers often build 'leave it at the front door' literally as 앞문에 두세요, but 앞문 means the physical 'front door (leaf)' of a building, whereas 문 앞 means 'in front of the door' — the location you want is 문 앞에 (door + 앞 'front-space' + 에 'at'). Getting the order wrong (앞문 vs 문 앞) is the classic slip.

usage: 존댓말 — complaint to a neighbor, staff, or stranger
반말 — to a friend, family, or roommate
격식 — written complaint to 관리실 or a formal report
It's that the upstairs unit is so loud…
Trailing -서요 softens it into a polite lead-in to a request
examples:
너무 시끄러워요.
죄송합니다, 조심할게요.
It's too loud. — Sorry, we'll be careful.
The bare complaint and the apology you hope to get
밤늦게 음악 소리가 너무 시끄러워요. 좀 줄여 주시겠어요?
The music is way too loud late at night. Could you turn it down a bit?
Everyday neighbor complaint paired with a polite request
안녕하세요, 아래층인데요. 밤마다 너무 시끄러워서 잠을 못 자겠어요.
Hi, I'm from downstairs — it's so loud every night I can't sleep.
Real doorstep complaint: 아래층인데요 identifies you first
nuance: You say this to flag noise — to a neighbor at the door, to staff in a public place, or as a written complaint. With a stranger keep 존댓말 (시끄러워요); to a friend it's 시끄러워; a formal report swaps to the noun 소음 + 심하다 ('the noise is severe'). The dividing line with the near-synonym 조용히 해 주세요 ('please be quiet') is direction: 시끄러워요 describes the problem (it IS loud), while 조용히 해 주세요 requests the fix — Koreans usually soften by stating the problem first, then the request. The English-speaker trap is treating 시끄럽다 like a verb you 'do'; it's an adjective (descriptive verb), so you never say 시끄러워 해요. Also, leading straight with a blunt 시끄러워요! to a neighbor sounds aggressive — open with 안녕하세요, 아래층인데요 ('I'm from downstairs') so it lands as a neighborly heads-up, not an attack.

english: Please keep it down a little
usage: 존댓말 — to a neighbor or stranger; 좀 softens the request
반말 — to a friend, sibling, or roommate
It's late, so please keep it down.
Adding 밤이라 ('since it's night') gives the request a reason
examples:
조용히 좀 해 주세요.
아, 죄송해요.
Please keep it down. — Oh, sorry.
The core request and the apology it usually gets
여기 도서관이에요. 조용히 좀 해 주세요.
This is a library. Please keep it down.
Stating the place first makes the request feel reasonable
죄송한데, 애들이 자고 있어서요. 조용히 좀 해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
Sorry, but my kids are sleeping — I'd really appreciate it if you kept it down.
Real polite neighbor ask: 죄송한데 opens, -면 감사하겠습니다 closes
nuance: This is the request form of a noise complaint, said to a neighbor, a loud stranger, or in a quiet venue. 조용히 = 'quietly', 해 주세요 = 'please do (for me)', and the little 좀 ('a little / please') is what makes it polite rather than a command — dropping 좀 makes it noticeably sharper. Register climbs 조용히 좀 해 → 조용히 좀 해 주세요 → 조용히 해 주시겠어요?; the last (a yes/no question) is the gentlest. Versus 시끄러워요, which merely describes the noise, this one asks for the fix, so Koreans often pair them: 너무 시끄러워요. 조용히 좀 해 주세요. The English-speaker mistake is the bare imperative 조용히 해 ('be quiet') to a stranger — in English 'please be quiet' sounds fine, but Korean without 좀 and 주세요 sounds like scolding a child; always cushion it with 좀 … 주세요 for anyone you don't know.

usage: 존댓말 — reporting to a landlord, staff, or 관리실
반말 — to a friend, family, or roommate
격식 — formal report, message, or written notice
Adding -ㄴ 것 같아요 ('seems') hedges when you're not 100% sure
examples:
고장 났어요.
언제부터요?
It's broken. — Since when?
The bare report and the natural follow-up question
세탁기가 갑자기 고장 났어요. 어떻게 해야 돼요?
The washing machine suddenly broke. What should I do?
갑자기 ('suddenly') is the usual lead-in for a breakdown
관리실이죠? 저희 집 인터폰이 고장 나서 전화드렸어요.
Is this the management office? I'm calling because our intercom is broken.
Real call: 고장 나서 ('because it broke') sets up the reason
nuance: 고장 나다 is the go-to phrase for a machine or appliance that stopped working — elevators, boilers, washing machines, intercoms, your phone. It pairs with the subject + 가/이 (보일러가 고장 났어요). To a landlord or office it's 존댓말 (났어요); among family 났어; a written notice uses 고장이 났습니다. The key dividing line: 고장 나다 is for things with a mechanism, while 망가지다 means 'got wrecked/ruined' and covers physical breakage of any object (a toy, a zipper, a relationship) — a glass that shatters is 깨졌어요, not 고장 났어요. The English-speaker trap is mapping 'broken' onto 부러졌어요 ('snapped in two', like a bone or stick) for an appliance — a TV that won't turn on is 고장 났어요, never 부러졌어요. Also note it's intransitive: the thing 고장 나다 ('breaks'); you don't 'break' it with this verb — to say you broke something, that's 고장 냈어요 (causative) or 망가뜨렸어요.

usage: 존댓말 — to a landlord, repair tech, or 관리실
반말 — to a friend or family member; 고치다 is the casual verb
I'd like to request a repair, please.
격식 — very polite; 부탁드립니다 for a formal request
Around when could it be repaired?
Natural follow-up asking for a repair timeline
examples:
수리 좀 해 주세요.
네, 기사님 보내 드릴게요.
Please get it fixed. — Sure, I'll send a technician.
The request and the office's standard response
보일러가 고장 났는데 수리 좀 해 주세요.
The boiler's broken — could you have it fixed?
Pairs naturally after stating what 고장 났어요
지난번에 말씀드린 곳인데요, 아직 수리가 안 돼서요. 빨리 좀 해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
It's the place I mentioned last time — it still isn't fixed, so I'd appreciate it if you could hurry.
Real follow-up chasing an overdue repair, kept polite
nuance: This requests a repair from a landlord, building office, or service center. 수리 is the Sino-Korean noun 'repair' and pairs with 하다, so 수리(를) 해 주세요 = 'please do the repair'; the casual everyday equivalent is the pure-Korean verb 고치다 (고쳐 주세요). The register split is also a word split: in 존댓말 to officials, 수리해 주세요 / 수리 부탁드려요 sounds proper; in 반말 to a friend you'd say 고쳐 줘, almost never 수리해 줘. The dividing line with 고치다: both mean 'fix', but 수리 implies a professional/paid repair of a machine or building, while 고치다 is broader and can also mean 'correct/mend' (fix a habit, mend clothes). English speakers often reach for 'repair' as 리페어 or try 만들어 주세요 ('make it') — 만들다 is 'create from scratch', wrong for fixing; use 수리해 주세요 or 고쳐 주세요. Adding 좀 keeps the request soft and natural.

Dropping 주세요 (just 수리해) when asking staff — it becomes an order; soften to 수리 좀 해 주세요 / 부탁드려요.

usage: 존댓말 — neighbor or staff directing you to 관리실
반말 — to a friend, family, or roommate
You can inquire with the management office.
격식 — formal phrasing; 문의하다 = make an inquiry
For that, you can just tell the management office.
Natural variant pointing you to the right place
examples:
엘리베이터가 안 돼요.
관리실에 전화해 보세요.
The elevator's not working. — Try calling the management office.
The bare problem and the standard 'who to call' answer
주차 문제는 저도 잘 몰라서요. 관리실에 한번 전화해 보세요.
I'm not sure about the parking issue myself — try giving the management office a call.
한번 ('once / give it a try') softens the suggestion
택배가 자꾸 없어지면 관리실에 전화해서 CCTV 확인해 달라고 해 보세요.
If your parcels keep disappearing, try calling the office and asking them to check the CCTV.
Real advice chaining 전화해서 … 달라고 해 보세요 (call and request)
nuance: In a Korean apartment (아파트) or officetel, the 관리실 (management/superintendent's office) handles building problems — elevators, water, heating, parking, deliveries — so this is the line a neighbor gives you when something breaks. 관리실에 takes 에 ('to a place'); -해 보세요 = 'try doing', which makes it a gentle suggestion rather than a command. To a stranger it's 존댓말 (보세요); to a friend 봐; formally you'd say 관리실로 문의하세요. The nearest term is 경비실 (the security/guard booth at the gate): 경비실 watches the entrance and receives parcels, while 관리실 deals with maintenance and bills — for a broken boiler you want 관리실, not 경비실. English speakers often call it the 'office' and say 사무실, but 사무실 is a generic business office; a residential building's maintenance desk is specifically 관리실, and the staffer is 관리소장님 or 경비 아저씨.

english: There's no water / The water won't come out
usage: 존댓말 — reporting to 관리실, landlord, or staff
반말 — to a roommate or family member
격식 — formal/notice wording; 단수 = water supply cut
갑자기 frames it as an unexpected outage
examples:
물이 안 나와요.
잠시만요, 확인해 볼게요.
There's no water. — One moment, I'll check.
The bare report and the office's standard reply
아침부터 화장실 물이 안 나와요. 혹시 단수예요?
There's been no water in the bathroom since morning — is the supply cut off, maybe?
혹시 단수예요? checks if it's a planned outage
온수가 안 나와서 찬물로 씻었어요. 보일러 문제일까요?
No hot water came out so I washed with cold — could it be the boiler?
Real situation distinguishing 온수 (hot) from plain 물
nuance: This reports a water outage to your building office or landlord. 물이 안 나와요 = 'water + subject + doesn't come out' — 나오다 ('come out') is the verb for water/gas/electricity flowing from a tap or outlet, and 안 negates it. The distinction to learn: plain 물 covers all water, but 온수 = hot water and 냉수/찬물 = cold — if only the hot is out (a boiler issue) say 온수가 안 나와요, which points to a different fix than a full 단수 (supply cut). The English-speaker trap is translating 'the water doesn't work' as 물이 안 돼요 — 되다 ('work/function') suits machines, but water 'comes out', so it's 나와요. Saying 물이 없어요 is also wrong here: 없어요 = 'there isn't any (in stock)', fine for a water bottle, but a dead tap is 물이 안 나와요.

usage: 존댓말 — reporting to landlord or 관리실
반말 — to family or a roommate
I turned the boiler on but it's not working.
틀었는데 ('I turned it on but…') shows you already tried
examples:
보일러가 안 돼요.
에러 표시 떠 있어요?
The boiler isn't working. — Is an error showing?
The bare report and the diagnostic follow-up
날도 추운데 보일러가 안 돼서 집이 너무 추워요.
It's cold out and the boiler's not working, so the place is freezing.
Everyday complaint linking the cold to the broken heat
보일러를 아무리 틀어도 온수가 안 나와요. 사람 좀 보내 주실 수 있어요?
No matter how I run the boiler, no hot water comes out — could you send someone?
Real call: 아무리 …아도 ('no matter how') plus a request for a tech

english: How do I do the recycling separation?
usage: How do I separate the recycling?
존댓말 — asking a neighbor or 관리실
How do you do the recycling?
반말 — asking a friend or roommate
How should the recycling be sorted?
Which bin does this go in?
Practical extension asking where one item goes
examples:
분리수거 어떻게 해요?
요일 정해져 있어요.
How do I do the recycling? — There's a set day for it.
The bare question and a typical first answer
이사 와서 잘 몰라서요. 분리수거 어떻게 해요?
I just moved in and don't really know — how do I sort the recycling?
이사 와서 ('since I moved in') explains why you're asking
플라스틱이랑 비닐은 따로 버려야 돼요? 분리수거 처음이라 잘 몰라서요.
Do plastic and plastic film go separately? It's my first time sorting and I'm not sure.
Real question distinguishing 플라스틱 (hard) from 비닐 (film)
nuance: 분리수거 (separate-collection, i.e. sorted recycling) is a daily ritual in Korean apartments, with separate bins for 플라스틱, 캔, 유리, 종이, 비닐, and strict collection days — so newcomers genuinely need this question. 분리수거(를) 어떻게 해요? = 'how do I do the sorting?'; the verb is 하다, and you 버리다 ('throw out / put out') each item. To a neighbor it's 존댓말 (해요); to a friend 해; formally -하면 됩니까. The related word 음식물 쓰레기 (food waste) is collected separately again — don't fold it into 분리수거 in your head. The English-speaker trap is calling it 'recycling' as 재활용 only: 재활용 is the abstract concept 'recycling/reuse', whereas the household act of sorting-and-putting-out is 분리수거 — ask 분리수거 어떻게 해요, not 재활용 어떻게 해요. Also 비닐 (plastic film/bags) and 플라스틱 (rigid plastic) go in different piles; lumping them is the usual newcomer error.

usage: 존댓말 — classifying an item for someone
반말 — to a roommate or family member
Food waste must be disposed of separately.
격식 — building notice; 배출하다 = put out/discharge
Can you take out the food waste?
Everyday chore request to a housemate
examples:
이거 음식물이에요?
아니요, 그건 일반 쓰레기예요.
Is this food waste? — No, that's general trash.
The core sort question and the contrast with 일반 쓰레기
음식물 쓰레기는 물기 빼고 버려야 돼요.
You have to drain the liquid before throwing out food waste.
물기 빼고 ('drain the moisture') is the standard rule
달걀 껍데기랑 뼈는 음식물 아니에요. 일반 쓰레기로 버리세요.
Eggshells and bones aren't food waste — put them in general trash.
Real edge case: hard shells/bones go to 일반 쓰레기, not 음식물
nuance: 음식물 쓰레기 ('food-stuff garbage') is the compostable food-waste stream that Korean homes must separate from 일반 쓰레기 (general trash) and from 분리수거 recyclables — usually into a dedicated bin or a paid 음식물 봉투. You put it out with 버리다 or, formally, 배출하다. Saying what something is uses 이에요/예요; the chore request is 버려 줄래/주세요. The dividing line with 일반 쓰레기 is sharp and trips everyone: only soft, decomposable food counts — 달걀 껍데기 (eggshells), 뼈 (bones), 조개껍데기 (clam shells), tea bags, and onion skins are NOT 음식물 and must go to general trash. The English-speaker trap is thinking 'food waste = anything from the kitchen'; in Korea the test is 'could an animal eat it / will it rot', so hard shells and bones are excluded. Another slip is calling it 음식 쓰레기 — the correct compound is 음식물 쓰레기 (with 물).

usage: The noise from upstairs is hard to deal with.
존댓말 — describing the problem to a neighbor or office
The inter-floor noise is really bad.
반말 — venting to a friend or family member
I filed a complaint regarding inter-floor noise.
격식 — formal; 민원 = civil complaint, 넣다 = file
윗집 층간 소음 때문에 잠을 못 자요.
I can't sleep because of the noise from the unit above.
Naming 윗집 ('upstairs unit') pinpoints the source
examples:
층간 소음이 심해요.
관리실에 말해 보셨어요?
The inter-floor noise is bad. — Have you told the management office?
The bare complaint and the usual next step
윗집 발소리랑 의자 끄는 소리, 층간 소음이 너무 심해요.
Footsteps and chairs dragging from upstairs — the inter-floor noise is just too much.
Lists the typical culprits: 발소리, 의자 끄는 소리
층간 소음 때문에 직접 올라가지 말고 관리실 통해서 얘기하는 게 좋아요.
For inter-floor noise, it's better to go through the management office rather than confronting them directly.
Real advice: 직접 올라가지 말고 ('don't go up yourself')
nuance: 층간 소음 (literally 'between-floors noise') is a hugely common and emotionally charged issue in Korean apartment living — footsteps, dragged chairs, kids running — and it's the fixed term everyone uses, so a newcomer should know it as a set phrase, not build it word by word. 층 = floor, 간 = 'between', 소음 = noise. You describe it with 심하다 ('severe') and act via the 관리실 or a formal 민원 (civil complaint). The near-synonym is just 소음 ('noise'), but 층간 소음 specifically means the apartment up/down-stairs conflict, with all its social weight. The English-speaker trap is inventing 'floor noise' as 바닥 소리 (literally 'floor sound'), which Koreans won't recognize as the issue; the term is 층간 소음. A cultural note baked into the language: Koreans strongly advise handling it 관리실을 통해서 ('through the office') rather than confronting the neighbor directly, because direct 층간 소음 confrontations are notorious for escalating.

usage: 존댓말 — reporting to 관리실 or neighbors
반말 — to a friend or family member
The elevator is broken and under inspection.
격식 — posted notice wording; 점검 중 = under maintenance
Variant for when it halts/gets stuck rather than fully breaks
examples:
엘리베이터가 고장 났어요.
계단으로 가셔야겠네요.
The elevator's broken. — Looks like you'll have to take the stairs.
The bare report and the practical consequence
엘리베이터가 또 고장 났어요. 이번 주만 벌써 두 번째예요.
The elevator's broken again — that's already the second time this week.
또 ('again') plus a count, a common real complaint
안에 사람이 갇혔어요! 엘리베이터가 고장 났어요. 빨리 관리실에 연락해 주세요!
Someone's trapped inside! The elevator's broken — please call the office quickly!
Emergency: 갇혔어요 ('is trapped') raises the urgency
nuance: This is the practical report you make to the 관리실 or warn neighbors with when the lift is out — a real concern in tall Korean apartments. 엘리베이터 (loanword; some older people say 승강기) takes 가/이, and the breakdown verb is 고장 나다. To the office it's 존댓말 (났어요); to a friend 났어; a posted sign reads 고장 나서 점검 중입니다. May I ask what the passcode is?
격식/정중 — softer, very polite way to ask
Could you tell me the Wi-Fi password?
examples:
비밀번호가 뭐예요?
공일이삼사예요.
What's the passcode? — It's 01234.
The bare question; 공 = 0 read aloud in codes
현관 비밀번호가 뭐예요? 손에 짐이 많아서요.
What's the front-door code? My hands are full.
현관 ('entrance') specifies the door lock code
체크인했는데요, 도어록 비밀번호가 안내된 거랑 달라서요. 다시 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
I've checked in, but the door-lock code is different from what was given — could you tell me again?
Real Airbnb/officetel situation: 도어록 = the keypad lock

The near-synonym 암호 ('cipher/passcode') exists but feels technical or spy-ish; for everyday locks and Wi-Fi, Koreans say 비밀번호 (often shortened 비번 in casual speech).

The English-speaker trap is reaching for 패스워드 — understood, but native and natural is 비밀번호. Another trap is the digits: Koreans read door codes with 공 for 0 (공일공일 = 0101) and may say 별표 (the * key) or 우물 정자/샵 (#), so listen for those, not 'zero'.

mistakes: Defaulting to 패스워드 — it's understood but the natural word is 비밀번호 (casual 비번).
Reading 0 as 제로 in a code — Koreans say 공 (공일이삼 = 0123); using 제로 sounds off for door/phone codes.
Asking 비밀번호가 어디예요? — 어디 = 'where'; to ask the value use 뭐예요? or 어떻게 되나요?.

usage: 존댓말 — inviting a guest, neighbor, or visitor inside
Come on in for a bit.
반말 — to a friend or younger person
Would you like to come in for a moment?
일단 ('first of all') warmly ushers them in
examples:
잠깐 들어오세요.
아니에요, 여기서 받을게요.
Come in for a moment. — Oh no, I'll take it here.
The bare invite and a polite decline at the door
밖에서 얘기하기 그러니까 잠깐 들어오세요.
It's awkward to talk out here, so come in for a bit.
얘기하기 그러니까 ('since it's awkward to talk') gives the reason
어머, 비 많이 오는데 잠깐 들어오세요. 차 한잔 드시고 가세요.
Oh my, it's pouring — come in for a moment. Have a cup of tea before you go.
Real neighborly warmth: invite + 드시고 가세요 ('have some and go')
nuance: This is the warm invitation a host gives at the door — to a neighbor returning something, a delivery person, or a guest you want to usher in out of the cold or rain. 잠깐 = 'for a moment/briefly', 들어오세요 = 'please come in' (들어오다, 'enter, come in', from the listener-toward-speaker direction). To most people it's 존댓말 (들어오세요); to a close friend 들어와; the politest is 잠시 들어오시겠어요? (a question is softer). The verb pair to keep straight is 들어오다 ('come in', toward the speaker, what a host says) vs 들어가다 ('go in', away from the speaker) — a host at home always says 들어오세요, never 들어가세요 (which would mean 'go in, away from me'). The English-speaker trap is exactly that direction error, plus translating 'come in' as the bare 와요 ('come') without 들어-, which loses the 'into the space' meaning. Note Korean homes are shoes-off, so the invitation implies stepping up past the 현관; a guest may answer 신발 벗어야 돼요? ('should I take my shoes off?').

english: Please take your shoes off before coming in
usage: Please take your shoes off and come in.
존댓말 — host telling a guest the house rule
Take your shoes off and come in.
반말 — to a friend or younger visitor
You can take your shoes off and come in.
격식 — polite/neutral, e.g. a posted notice or formal host
examples:
신발 벗고 들어오세요.
아, 네!
Please take your shoes off. — Oh, sure!
The bare house rule and the guest's quick agreement
여기 현관에서 신발 벗고 들어오시면 돼요.
You can take your shoes off here at the entrance and come in.
현관 names the spot where shoes come off
양말 안 신으셨으면 여기 덧신 있어요. 신발 벗고 들어오세요.
If you're not wearing socks, there are guest socks here. Please take your shoes off and come in.
Real hosting touch: offering 덧신 (guest socks) with the rule
nuance: Removing shoes indoors is a firm rule in every Korean home, so a host says this routinely and a newcomer must both understand it and obey it. 신발 = shoes, 벗다 = take off (clothing/shoes), and -고 links it to 들어오세요 ('take off AND come in'). To a guest it's 존댓말 (벗고 들어오세요); to a friend 벗고 들어와. The verb to nail is 벗다 ('take off') vs its opposite 신다 ('put on', for footwear specifically) — you 신발을 벗다 to remove and 신발을 신다 to wear; note shoes/socks use 신다, not 입다 (which is for clothing on the torso). The English-speaker trap is using 입다/벗다 wrong for footwear ('take off shoes' as 신발을 입다 is impossible) and stepping up onto the raised floor (마루/거실) with shoes still on — the line between the 현관 (lowered entry) and the floor is exactly where shoes must come off. Forgetting and walking in shod is one of the most noticeable foreigner mistakes in Korea.

usage: 존댓말 — answering the door or intercom to an unknown caller
반말 — to family, or when you expect a friend
May I ask what brings you?
격식/정중 — softer, asks their purpose rather than identity
The typical answer you'll hear back through the door
examples:
(딩동) 누구세요?
택배입니다.
(Ding-dong) Who is it? — Delivery.
The bare intercom exchange when the bell rings
누구세요? 저희 집에 무슨 일이세요?
Who is it? What do you need from us?
Adding 무슨 일이세요? asks their business politely
밤늦게 모르는 사람이 벨을 눌러서 문 안 열고 누구세요? 하고 물었어요.
A stranger rang late at night, so without opening I asked 'who is it?' through the door.
Real safety habit: ask 누구세요? before opening
nuance: This is the phrase you say through a closed door or the 인터폰 (intercom) when someone rings — distinct in feel from answering the phone, though the words overlap. 누구세요? = 'who are you?' with the honorific 세요, polite enough for any stranger. To family it drops to 누구야?; a gentler, more formal alternative is 어떻게 오셨어요? ('what brings you?'), which asks purpose instead of bluntly demanding identity and is what you'd use for a guest you half-expect. The dividing line: 누구세요? is direct ('who?') and fine for an unknown buzz; 어떻게 오셨어요? is softer and better once you're opening the door to someone who looks legitimate. The English-speaker trap is answering a knock with 여보세요? — that's strictly the telephone 'hello' and sounds odd at a door; at the door it's 누구세요?. Another slip is 당신 누구예요?: 당신 ('you') sounds confrontational or even like a challenge to a stranger, so drop it — the subject-less 누구세요? is the natural, safe form.

usage: I just moved in next door.
존댓말 — greeting a neighbor as the new resident
반말 — to a friend or peer neighbor
격식 — formal greeting, e.g. to an older neighbor or 관리실
I hope we'll get along going forward.
The set phrase that almost always follows
examples:
안녕하세요, 옆집에 이사 왔어요.
아, 반가워요!
Hi, I just moved in next door. — Oh, nice to meet you!
The bare newcomer greeting and a warm reply
며칠 전에 이사 왔는데 인사가 늦었어요. 잘 부탁드려요.
I moved in a few days ago — sorry the greeting's late. I hope we get along.
인사가 늦었어요 ('greeting is late') is a polite touch
이사 왔는데 떡 좀 돌리려고요. 시끄럽게 했으면 죄송해요.
I just moved in and wanted to share some rice cakes. Sorry if we were noisy.
Real custom: 떡 돌리다 (sharing 떡) as a moving-in greeting
nuance: Greeting the neighbors as a new arrival is a real social step in Korea, and 이사 왔어요 ('I have moved in / come by moving') is the core line — said at the door to 옆집 (next door), 윗집/아랫집 (upstairs/downstairs), or the 경비/관리실. 이사(를) 오다 = 'to move in (toward here)'; note the directional verb 오다 ('come') because you've arrived where you now are — 이사 갔어요 (with 가다, 'go') means you moved OUT/away, the opposite. To neighbors it's 존댓말 (왔어요); to a peer 이사 왔어; formally 이사 오게 되었습니다. It's almost always followed by the set phrase 잘 부탁드립니다 ('please treat me well / let's get along'), which has no literal English equivalent — leaving it off feels abrupt. The English-speaker trap is exactly the 오다/가다 direction error (saying 이사 갔어요 to a new neighbor implies you're leaving), plus translating 'move' as 움직이다 ('move physically/budge'), which is wrong: relocating houses is 이사하다.
